## Definitions

- [statement] Punding is a related repetitive, non-goal-directed behaviour, such as repeatedly sorting, assembling or disassembling objects; it and DDS are related to, but distinguishable from, the usual gambling, shopping, eating and sexual ICDs. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11098885/ · keywords: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6059034/

## How it works

- [statement] Dopamine dysregulation syndrome (DDS) involves compulsive use of dopamine replacement medication beyond motor requirements, with drug seeking or hoarding, social impairment and sometimes mood elevation; distress can emerge when doses are reduced. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1736875/ · keywords: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11098885/
- [statement] Dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome can complicate tapering, with anxiety, panic, depression or dysphoria, fatigue and pain; symptoms may be refractory to levodopa replacement. Its recognition matters because it can prevent successful agonist withdrawal. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5077247/ · keywords: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11098885/
- [statement] NICE recommends specialist cognitive behavioural therapy directed at ICDs when changing dopaminergic treatment is ineffective. A small randomized waiting-list-controlled trial supports short-term improvement in patient symptom severity. (medium confidence) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3598451/
- [statement] A clinical review states that non-pharmacological approaches such as limiting access to credit cards, the Internet or gambling venues should be implemented but are usually not enough on their own; a management table notes that carer involvement in surveillance can facilitate earlier detection of ICDs and that caregivers or family may participate in management when symptoms persist. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5077247/ · keywords: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11098885/

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] In Parkinson’s disease, clinically important impulse control disorders include compulsive gambling, shopping, sexual behaviour and binge eating; these behaviours can cause serious financial and psychosocial harm. (medium confidence) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6059034/
- [statement] Dopamine agonist exposure is a major ICD risk factor, but ICDs can occur with other dopaminergic therapies; absence of agonist treatment does not eliminate risk. (medium confidence) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6059034/
- [statement] The French DIGPD longitudinal cohort found independent associations of greater lifetime average dopamine agonist dose and longer exposure with ICDs. This is observational evidence; individual susceptibility and studies with conflicting dose associations limit a universal dose threshold. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6059034/ · keywords: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11098885/
- [statement] NICE NG71 states that when dopamine agonist therapy is started, people and, as appropriate, their family members and carers should be given oral and written information about the increased risk of impulse control disorders, which may be concealed by the person affected, and that the discussion should be recorded; a clinical review states that all patients with PD should be advised about the potential risk of behavioural addictions, especially following dopamine agonist therapy. (medium confidence) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11098885/
- [statement] NICE NG71 states that, if a person with Parkinson's disease has developed a problematic impulse control disorder, advice should be sought from a healthcare professional with specialist expertise in Parkinson's disease before modifying dopaminergic therapy, and describes first gradually reducing the dopamine agonist while monitoring both ICD response and withdrawal; a management review tabulates reducing the oral dopamine agonist while observing for resolution of ICDs, loss of motor control and dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome. (medium confidence) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5077247/
- [statement] The CBT trial randomized 27 patients to intervention and 17 to waiting-list control. Its small size, six-month follow-up, inability to blind participants and assessors, and lack of an active control limit certainty; caregiver burden and distress did not improve significantly. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3598451/ · keywords: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation
- [statement] Naltrexone has not established overall efficacy for PD-related ICDs: the 2015 management review reports a negative primary global-response outcome but improved secondary QUIP-RS scores, whereas the 2024 review summarizes the trial as a failure to improve ICDs. Secondary scale improvement should not be represented as definitive treatment success. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5077247/ · keywords: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11098885/

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] In DIGPD, among 306 participants without baseline ICDs who had follow-up, estimated cumulative ICD incidence over five years was 46.1% (95% CI 37.4–55.7): 51.5% in ever dopamine-agonist users versus 12.4% in never users. These are cohort-specific cumulative incidences, not a general population prevalence or a DDS estimate. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6059034/ · keywords: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation
- [statement] Previous impulsive or addictive behaviour, alcohol or smoking history, and younger age are described as risk factors for ICDs in Parkinson's disease; these are risk associations rather than diagnostic rules. (medium confidence) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations · keywords: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11098885/

## Facts and statements

- [statement] A 2024 clinical review distinguishes DDS management from usual ICD management: DDS may require reducing levodopa or fast-acting apomorphine exposure, with monitoring for motor deterioration and withdrawal and sometimes inpatient multidisciplinary care. This is review guidance, not evidence of a proven universally effective regimen. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11098885/ · keywords: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation

## Research summary — Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation

Impulse control disorders in Parkinson’s disease include harmful gambling, shopping, sexual behaviour and binge eating. Dopamine dysregulation syndrome involves compulsive medication overuse; punding involves repetitive, purposeless activity. Dopamine agonists carry a major ICD risk, although other dopaminergic therapy can also be implicated. Prevention requires candid patient and family counselling and repeated behavioural review. Management generally starts with specialist-guided gradual agonist reduction, while watching motor control and withdrawal. DDS can require a different medication-reduction strategy. Specialist cognitive behavioural therapy may help persistent ICDs, but trial limitations and endpoint-dependent drug results argue against overstating treatment certainty.

## Source disagreement — Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation

Naltrexone interpretation depends on the endpoint: the 2015 review describes a negative primary outcome with secondary QUIP-RS improvement, while the 2024 review summarizes failure to improve ICDs. These are different readings of the same trial, not independent efficacy replications.
